concepts.name: Limits of computation
concepts.question: What can a machine actually do?
concepts.description: Move between computability, reductions, circuits and the resources needed to solve a problem.
concepts.takeaway: Search is not always a decision.
concepts.explanation:
A solution can be easy to check even when a search has no known stopping point. For a finite Boolean formula, exhausting all assignments eventually yields YES or NO. For an integer polynomial, expanding the search box finds any existing solution, but an unsuccessful run may continue forever.

Turing supplies the language for this distinction; Julia Robinson’s work helps carry it into arithmetic. Ask first whether a total algorithm exists, then what resources it needs. Decidability and efficiency are separate questions.

bridges.why: A witness can settle a YES instance without giving a method that decides every instance.
Encoding computation with polynomials turns a question about programs into a question about integer solutions.

concepts.name: Proof & verification
concepts.question: Can checking be easier than solving?
concepts.description: Read the profiles on formal proofs, interactive verification and probabilistically checkable proofs.
concepts.takeaway: A witness and a search are different objects.
concepts.explanation:
A proposed Hamiltonian cycle can be checked by verifying its edges and its visits to vertices. The certificate tells the checker where to look. Finding such a certificate is a different task, and the absence of one proposed certificate does not prove that none exists.

Interactive proofs replace a single handed-over witness with a conversation and a verifier’s random choices. Zero knowledge adds a further demand about what that conversation reveals. Neither interaction nor a short convincing transcript by itself establishes zero knowledge.

sources.label: Goldwasser, Micali & Rackoff · The Knowledge Complexity of Interactive Proof Systems

bridges.why: Verification conditions become meaningful only after the computation and resource bounds of the checker are specified.
A proof may convince while controlling disclosure. Secrecy is an additional property, not a synonym for correctness.

concepts.name: Approximation & optimization
concepts.question: How close to the best can we get?
concepts.description: Explore the conversation between approximation algorithms, relaxations and hardness results.
concepts.takeaway: A good answer needs a yardstick.
concepts.explanation:
For the five-cycle, four crossing edges are optimal: cutting all five would require a two-coloring of an odd cycle. This small example gives both a construction and an upper bound. On larger graphs, certifying closeness to the optimum is often the difficult part.

Goemans and Williamson relax MAX-CUT into a problem about vectors and round a solution back to a cut. Approximation ratios compare the resulting value with the unknown optimum; they are not percentages of instances solved exactly. Nonnegative edge weights are part of the standard guarantee.

bridges.why: Vector geometry can make a discrete optimization problem easier to bound before rounding.
A certificate of a good feasible solution differs from a certificate that no much better solution exists.

concepts.name: Local views, global structure
concepts.question: What can a neighborhood reveal?
concepts.description: Follow refinement, logical locality and sparsity through the graph-theory profiles.

concepts.name: Randomness & probability
concepts.question: When is chance a mathematical tool?
concepts.description: Find random constructions, dependent events and the algorithms that use or replace randomness.

concepts.name: The polynomial viewpoint
concepts.question: What happens when logic becomes algebra?
concepts.description: Explore arithmetization, polynomial identities, arithmetic circuits and algebraic certificates.

concepts.name: Symmetry & sameness
concepts.question: When are two objects really the same?
concepts.description: Read about permutations, invariants, group actions and graph isomorphism.
concepts.takeaway: A new drawing need not be a new graph.
concepts.explanation:
A graph isomorphism is a bijection of vertices preserving adjacency. Moving the vertices on the page or changing their names does not change that structure. A useful invariant must therefore survive these operations.

An invariant is a test, not necessarily a complete description: the same degree sequence does not guarantee isomorphism. For example, one six-cycle and two disjoint triangles both have six degree-two vertices, yet only the first is connected. This is why refinement and stronger structural methods matter.

sources.label: Babai · Graph Isomorphism in Quasipolynomial Time

bridges.why: Matching local signatures may conceal different global structures; connectivity is already a simple example.
Confusability graphs translate a communication question into a structural one.

concepts.name: Counting & combinatorics
concepts.question: Why can counting be harder than finding?
concepts.description: Find counting problems, generating functions, combinatorial structures and enumeration.

concepts.name: Information & secrecy
concepts.question: What can be sent without being revealed?
concepts.description: Explore information, coding, cryptography and proof systems that protect secrets.
concepts.explanation:
Represent a bit by either 000 or 111. Each valid word has a neighborhood of strings one flip away; the two neighborhoods do not overlap. That separation makes correction possible. Two flips can cause a wrong answer, so the error assumption is part of the claim.

Hamming studies explicit codes and decoding. Shannon asks which rates a channel can sustain reliably. Blackwell asks how an observation changes the decisions available to its recipient. These are connected meanings of information, with different success criteria.

sources.label: Hamming · Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes (1950)
Shannon · A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948)
Blackwell · Equivalent Comparisons of Experiments (1953), abstract and publication record

bridges.why: Distance and confusability turn messages into geometric or graph objects whose structure matters.
A signal is useful because of what can be inferred or decided from it, not only how many bits it contains.

concepts.name: Learning & intelligence
concepts.question: What does it mean to learn a rule?
concepts.description: Find profiles about learning from examples, reasoning and the representation of knowledge.
concepts.takeaway: Better information means more possible decisions.
concepts.explanation:
Imagine holding a perfect signal while another observer sees a randomly corrupted version. You can imitate their observation and then use their decision rule. They cannot generally reverse the corruption. This simulation explains one direction of Blackwell’s comparison of experiments.

Learning a rule from examples adds its own questions about the hypothesis class, sample size, and generalization. The connection is a reading bridge: a more informative experiment is not automatically a faster learning algorithm.

sources.label: Blackwell · Equivalent Comparisons of Experiments (1953), abstract and publication record
Bickel · David Blackwell: An explorer in mathematics and statistics (2020)

bridges.why: Channels describe both communication and the observations available to a decision-maker.
A useful statistical rule may still be expensive to compute; information and computational resources are different constraints.
